prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B039 first. Band topology with a Z2 invariant is a simple, general mechanism: time-reversal symmetry plus spin-orbit coupling forces robust boundary states that survive non-magnetic disorder. It was written down cleanly by Kane and Mele, tested in HgTe wells by Molenkamp's group through quantised edge conductance and nonlocal transport, and has since been confirmed by independent groups and carried into 3D materials, photonic, mechanical and cold-atom systems. About twenty years of reproduction with a stable interpretation make it mature, and nobody in round 1 called it premature. The 2016 prize treated topological defects, phase transitions and Chern-number quantisation; the time-reversal-protected Z2 structure is a different organising principle. The round-1 exchange pushed me to take the attribution problem more seriously, and I now think it should be handled in the citation wording rather than left as a standing weakness.
statement.case_against: The credit is still the weak point. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the host that Molenkamp's experiment tested, and Zhang's death does not make the omission less visible. Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy, Hasan and Cava established the 3D case, and with a three-name limit no trio covers the 2D and 3D stories together. A prize worded for the 2D quantum spin Hall effect leaves the 3D pioneers as an acknowledged adjacent achievement, and an outside reader could still call that arbitrary. By contrast B022 has a cleaner two-name credit. I am also working from memory on priority chronology, and my preference for clean theory with a mechanism may lead me to undervalue measurement-driven candidates; I accept that if the committee weights precision above novelty, B022 is a reasonable winner.

responses.point: Eriksson argues the attribution problem should be settled in the citation wording, and that the trio is defensible but not uncontested, with the 3D case as an acknowledged adjacent achievement.
responses.response: I now agree with this more firmly than in round 1. My round-1 citation, 'topological insulators' without qualification, invited the objection that we ignored the 3D work. I have narrowed it to the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators with the experimental discovery of the effect in HgTe wells. This is the only way to make Kane, Mele and Molenkamp a coherent set: Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 classification and the prediction, Molenkamp the observation. It does not erase Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and I would ask the Secretary to obtain external advice on exactly how much the HgTe proposal weighs in the priority record. If the experts say the proposal was decisive, I would have to reconsider, since I cannot fit four names.

responses.point: Kroll argues the B022 citation should be built around the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 level so that it is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes, and notes that single-ion clocks compete on accuracy.
responses.response: That is the right way to write B022 and it would answer part of my overlap worry: the lattice lets many atoms be interrogated with no recoil or Doppler shift, which is a genuinely separate idea from the comb or ion control. I still do not think the citation can fully remove the boundary question, because the best single-ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) reach comparable accuracy, so the claim that the lattice is what made 10^-18 possible is contestable even for the lattice-specific story. On the pending redefinition of the second, I agree with you and Danielsson that the physics does not depend on it. My remaining difference is weighting: a clock prize is for a better instrument, and I rank a new organising principle higher, though I would not oppose B022.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether a B022 prize rests on new fundamental physics (millimetre redshift, constants, many-body clock physics) and which of Katori's demonstration and Ye's accuracy record is essential; she also admits her own taste for the unexpected cuts against B022.
responses.response: Your own taste for the unexpected is the point I would lean on. Where I accept your case is that millimetre-scale redshift measurements and constant-variation bounds are real results about nature, not just a smaller error bar. But so far these are bounds and demonstrations, not a changed picture of what a phase of matter can be, and the new many-body clock physics is still young. On the two-name question, I think Katori's proposal and early demonstration and Ye's accuracy record are both needed, so the pair is coherent; that is why I regard B022 as the cleanest credit on the shortlist and keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Olsson says the lattice clock is a distinct invention with its own original experiment, that the 2005 and 2012 prizes do not cover it, and that the experimental record of topological insulators shows about twenty years of confirmation compared with eight for moire materials.
responses.response: I agree on both points and they sharpen my own position. Twenty years of independent confirmation is exactly why I place B039 above B035, where the pairing mechanism is still open and the phases are device-dependent. On B022 I accept your argument that the lattice idea is not covered by the comb or ion prizes, and I withdraw the stronger form of my round-1 overlap objection. What remains is a difference in kind: you weigh the invention and realisation of the instrument, I weigh the organising principle. That is a real disagreement about criteria, not about facts, and I do not think it can be settled by counting support.

responses.point: Danielsson wants the B039 citation confined to the 2D case, and asks whether the committee can show that its claim rests on the spin Hall effect and Z2 insulators rather than on all of topological insulators.
responses.response: I accept this confinement and have adopted it. My caveat is that 'Z2 topological insulators' in the citation already names a structure that was first defined for 2D and then generalised to 3D by Fu, Kane and Mele. I would keep that wording because it states the concept Kane and Mele introduced, while the experimental half of the citation is limited to HgTe quantum wells. That keeps the credit accurate without claiming the whole 3D programme. If the committee prefers to drop the Z2 phrase to avoid any such implication, I could accept the narrower wording, but I would not accept dropping Kane or Mele.

uncertainties: Whether external experts will judge the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal as decisive enough that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp cannot stand alone as the credited set.
Whether the committee weights conceptual novelty over metrological impact; this decides between B039 and B022 and is a difference in criteria rather than in facts.
Whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the 3D topological insulators are one achievement or two, which no three-person set resolves.
I am working from memory for priority details, and have not verified them independently.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. No conflict with any credited candidate for B039, B022 or B025 is apparent from my profile, and I found no collaboration with any shortlisted candidate. Gothenburg physics and Chalmers physics are closely linked and Johansson and Olsson are Gothenburg-based colleagues, which matters only for B023 and not for my preferred part. I am not recusing myself from any shortlisted ballot.
